strengths: MaskSub offers a simple, technically coherent way to combine supervised learning with strong masking: a shared network learns from labels on full images and detached predictions on masked views. It adds no inference overhead or separate teacher parameters. The practical contribution and supporting experiments warrant weak acceptance.

Improvements persist over strong training recipes. Table 1 reports gains of 0.6–0.7 percentage points across ViT sizes at 400 epochs and 0.3–0.5 points at 800 epochs. Repeated runs support the central result: Table A.13 improves ViT-B from 83.46±0.04 to 84.08±0.02.

The paper meaningfully accounts for additional computation. Table 8 reports 84.1% for MaskSub versus 83.7% for longer baseline training at approximately equal cost, 25 versus 26 GPU days. Table 9 also shows better accuracy and lower measured training cost than CoSub in the evaluated setting.

Evaluation breadth is a substantial strength: MAE, BEiT v2 and CLIP fine-tuning; ResNet and Swin training; classification transfer; segmentation; detection; and robustness. ADE20K gains of 0.4–0.6 mIoU and the ViT-B ImageNet-A improvement from 36.8% to 41.9% demonstrate value beyond standard ImageNet accuracy.

The appendix provides useful ablations of distillation, mask ratios, loss weights, and additional branches, alongside repeated runs for several experiments. Algorithm 1 and Tables B.1–B.2 explain the implementation and training recipes, and a code link is provided. These details make the central vision experiments reasonably reproducible.
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is narrower than the framing suggests. With a detached teacher distribution, Equation 3's cross-entropy has the same optimization gradient as KL consistency regularization. Thus, Section 2's distinction between distillation and UDA's consistency loss does not establish a new objective. The contribution primarily concerns the masking design, computational implementation, and extensive empirical validation; a direct comparison with an adapted UDA-style baseline would better isolate that contribution.

The proposed 'automatic difficulty control' is plausible but not established by the aggregate loss and gradient plots. Small consistency gradients indicate agreement between views, which need not imply correct predictions. The claim that masking is effectively applied exclusively to successfully predicted examples is therefore too strong. Table A.7 also shows improvement without masking, from 77.4% to 78.4%, indicating that part of the benefit comes from the broader self-distillation procedure.

The benefits have meaningful limits. In Table A.10, adding MaskSub during fine-tuning reduces ViT-B CIFAR-100 accuracy from 91.89% to 89.55%. Section 4.2 explicitly states that CLIP fine-tuning's best checkpoint matches the baseline despite better final-epoch accuracy. Furthermore, ResNet and Swin require approximately double the training computation because token removal is unavailable. These findings qualify the claims of consistently beneficial, inexpensive additional regularization.

Some secondary comparisons are less decisive than the main DeiT experiments. Table 6 mixes training recipes and, in one entry, architectures, so its rankings cannot fully isolate the self-distillation method, although some RSB-matched comparisons are included. Several small gains, particularly the 0.1-point BEiT v2 improvements, lack reported variability; the repeated-run evidence elsewhere should not be extended to these results.

Minor reporting issues remain distinct from the substantive concerns: Table 7 labels both initial dataset columns CIFAR100, and the BCE extension is described as replacing softmax with sigmoid without explicitly giving the complete binary loss. GLUE training hyperparameters are also much less fully specified than the vision recipes.
